suggested_french: Je saigne beaucoup et ca ne s'arrete pas.
suggestion_note: v1 'un saignement abondant qui ne s'arrete pas', folded into an utterance. NO SECOND PHRASING: HT01's French ('un saignement qui ne s'arrete pas malgre la pression') is the wording its collapse ruling reserved for the speaker, and the Kinyarwanda second_phrasing slot here is empty. EX16 first is the only row in the spine that carries one. Proposing French text into a slot the speaker has not filled would invent it — the same reason English left EX22's alone.

suggested_french: {REL} saigne beaucoup et ca ne s'arrete pas.
J'ai une plaie profonde qui saigne beaucoup.
suggestion_note: v1 text with the subject folded in. 'profonde' and 'infectee' agree with 'plaie', a fixed feminine, so this whole domain's wound vocabulary is FR-1 safe by construction.

suggested_french: {REL} a une plaie profonde qui saigne beaucoup.
Mon nez saigne et ca ne s'arrete pas.
suggestion_note: LEADS WITH THE NOSE, deliberately, and for the reason English did: in Kinyarwanda EX18 is every word of EX20 in order, so the two are one phrase group there. Measured here rather than assumed — the v1 French pair does not nest either way, so leading with the nose is belt and braces rather than the fix. It also mirrors the speaker's own 'Amazuru yanjye ...', which puts the nose in subject position, and the body-part subject is the FR-1 construction anyway. Note the Kinyarwanda noun changed on 2026-09-05 from 'amaraso' to 'imyuna' on a speaker's ruling; French has one word for a nosebleed and no equivalent choice to get wrong.

suggested_french: Le nez de {REL} saigne et ca ne s'arrete pas.
suggestion_note: Body part as subject, {REL} as possessor — matches '{REL} arimo kuva imyuna mu mazuru' and is FR-1 safe.

suggested_french: J'ai une blessure a la tete apres une chute.
suggestion_note: v1 text, subject folded in, otherwise unchanged. v1-cross-language-parity.md records EX21 as the one position where ENGLISH is the outlier — it alone adds a 'bad' fall, while ki/fr/sw say only 'a fall'. So the French here is already the correct side of that split and is deliberately not aligned to the English.

suggested_french: {REL} a une blessure a la tete apres une chute.
J'ai une plaie infectee, elle est rouge et il y a du pus.
suggestion_note: v1 text as an utterance. NO SECOND PHRASING, same as EX18: HT06's French ('une plaie rouge, enflee et qui coule du pus') is reserved by its collapse ruling and the Kinyarwanda slot is empty.

suggested_french: {REL} a une plaie infectee, elle est rouge et il y a du pus.
J'ai fait une chute et maintenant j'ai tres mal.
suggestion_note: FR-1: 'je suis tombe' would be masculine for a patient of unknown gender, so the fall is expressed with 'faire une chute', which takes no agreement. This construction is used again at HT05 and is the domain's main FR-1 workhorse.

suggested_french: {REL} a fait une chute et a maintenant tres mal.
J'ai une plaie profonde et on voit l'os.
suggestion_note: FLAG CARRIED FORWARD from the English pass, unchanged and still unruled: HT02 and HT05 share the anchor 'BEC Module 2: approach to trauma' and disagree on urgency, CRITICAL against URGENT. It looks like a coarse module-level anchor over two real presentations, the CR02/CC04 shape. Not ruled here.

suggested_french: {REL} a une plaie profonde et on voit l'os.

suggestion_note: HELD, and the hold transfers unchanged. The Kinyarwanda reason is clinical, not lexical: whether a patient confused enough to be triaged this way can report their own confusion is rule 11's question, and it is the same question in French. Sheet draft D098 is left in place as the record of what is not accepted.

suggested_french: {REL} a recu un coup a la tete et, depuis, vomit et n'a plus les idees claires.
suggestion_note: Drafted while the first stays held — an observer reporting confusion has none of the first person's problem, the same split English made here and at NE06 and CC01/CC02. FR-1 RULING WITH THREE MORE USES: 'confus' inflects, so it cannot sit in a {REL} phrase. The replacement is either the noun 'de la confusion' or the idiom 'ne plus avoir les idees claires'; the idiom is the better patient register and is used here, at NE06 and at CC02.

suggested_french: J'ai une brulure sur une grande partie du corps.
suggestion_note: Sheet draft D100, subject folded in. 'brulure' is a noun, so nothing agrees.

suggested_french: {REL} a une brulure sur une grande partie du corps.
J'ai fait une chute et ma jambe est tordue, mais je ne crois pas qu'elle soit cassee.
suggestion_note: HOLD LIFTED BECAUSE THE SPEAKER AUTHORED IT ON 2026-09-05, not because French found a way round the block. The English brief still holds both HT05 rows and still says 'arm'; it is the stale record here. Three things follow the speaker's 'Naguye, ukuguru kuragoramye ariko sinumva ko kuvunitse.' rather than the English or sheet draft D102. It is the LEG, not the arm — the gloss says 'limb' and the speaker chose the leg. The phrase DISCLAIMS THE FRACTURE inside itself, which is rule 11's axis stated in Kinyarwanda: deformity is what a patient perceives, a fracture is the diagnosis. And 'chute' rather than 'je suis tombe' keeps it FR-1 clean, while 'tordue' and 'cassee' agree with 'jambe', a fixed feminine.

suggested_french: {REL} a fait une chute et sa jambe est tordue, mais elle ne semble pas cassee.
suggestion_note: The Kinyarwanda third is not authored yet; drafted from the speaker's first, as English did before the first existed. 'sa jambe' is FR-2 and both participles agree with 'jambe'.

suggested_french: Je me suis fait mordre par un serpent.
suggestion_note: FR-1 REDRAFT, and the interesting one. Sheet draft D106 was 'mordu par un serpent' — masculine. The obvious repairs do not work: 'un serpent m'a mordu' agrees with the preceding direct object, and 'j'ai ete mordu' agrees with the subject, so both reintroduce the defect. 'se faire + infinitif' leaves the participle INVARIABLE and is ordinary patient speech. Worth keeping as the pattern for any passive-shaped event in this corpus.

suggested_french: {REL} s'est fait mordre par un serpent.
suggestion_note: Same invariable 'fait'; one sentence covers all eight relations.

suggested_french: J'ai une petite coupure et le saignement s'est arrete.
suggestion_note: Sheet draft D108 said 'qui ne saigne plus'; the speaker's 'amaraso yarahagaze' says the bleeding HAS STOPPED, which is the same claim more directly, and the English says it that way too. 's'est arrete' agrees with 'le saignement'.

suggested_french: {REL} a une petite coupure et le saignement s'est arrete.
